newsitem.title: USA: Astronaut looks forward to stay on troubled Mir.
newsitem.headline: Astronaut looks forward to stay on troubled Mir.

text.p: With the space shuttle's risky launch behind him, astronaut Michael Foale said on Friday he was looking forward to a calm and easy life aboard Russia's troubled Mir space station.
Foale, bound for a four-month stay aboard the increasingly decrepit orbiting outpost, said he had no qualms about living there.

"I was slightly nervous before launch because of the risks involved, but since those are all behind us right now, I feel perfectly at ease," the British-born astronaut told Britain's BBC television on Friday in an interview over NASA's live feed from the shuttle.
Foale and six crewmates blasted off from Florida before dawn on Thursday aboard the space shuttle Atlantis, headed for a docking with Mir on Friday night.

Foale, a 40-year-old astrophysicist who grew up in Cambridge, England and joined NASA in 1983 after completing his doctorate at Cambridge University, is to take the place of U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger aboard Mir.
Linenger, who joined the space station's crew in January, has endured a string of serious mechanical breakdowns, one of which triggered a brief but serious fire.

"There have been some problems, but none of these are ever big show stoppers," Foale said. "They are serious to some extent, but we can always continue to repair and improvise and work around those problems."

Foale added he was looking forward to "living calmly and easily in space," and although there were similarities between life on Mir and his time at a strict English boarding school, he said "it could be a less stressful experience."
Foale, who has an American mother and joint British-U.S. citizenship, has received additional training to help his cosmonaut crewmates maintain the 11-year-old space station.
Atlantis was speeding through space toward a link-up with Mir at 10:34 p.m. EDT on Friday (0234 GMT Saturday). It will be its sixth visit to the space complex.
On Friday morning, the $2 billion spaceship was trailing Mir by 1,800 miles (2,900 km) and was closing in by 310 miles (500 km) with every orbit of the Earth.
Foale and Linenger will swop places soon after the hatches between shuttle and Mir are opened at about 30 minutes past midnight EDT (0430 GMT).
If all goes according to plan, Linenger will return to Earth aboard Atlantis on May 24. His wife is expecting their second child in June.
Atlantis was also carrying a record 4,000 lbs (1,814 kg) of supplies and equipment to Mir, including repair gear to patch up a leaky cooling system and an oxygen generator, called Elektron.
The bulky generator, about the size of an electric water heater, will be one of the first items moved across to Mir.
"It is the number one transfer item," Jim Van Laak, deputy head of NASA's shuttle-Mir programme, said.
The Elektron was a last-minute addition to Atlantis' cargo. The Russian space authorities rushed it to the shuttle's launch site after problems with Mir's life support systems.
The device uses electricity to generate breathing oxygen from waste water and will provide a crucial backup to an older, ailing system.
Foale will become the fifth NASA astronaut to live on Mir. He will be followed by two more U.S. astronauts.
